```{python}
#| echo: false
import warnings
warnings.simplefilter("ignore", UserWarning)
```

The [GHRSST](https://www.ghrsst.org/) Multi-scale Ultra-high Resolution (MUR)
sea surface temperature analysis is a daily global grid at 0.01 degrees
(17999 x 36000 cells) from 2002-06-01. A cloud-optimised copy is published
on [source.coop](https://source.coop/ausantarctic/ghrsst-mur-v2) as five
Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs per day, one per variable, with a STAC catalogue
in stac-geoparquet form. The pipeline that produces it is
[AustralianAntarcticDivision/ghrsst-cogger](https://github.com/AustralianAntarcticDivision/ghrsst-cogger).

This page builds one multidimensional VRT over the whole collection from the
catalogue alone, then uses it for a regional map, a 24-year pixel series, the
start of the anomaly record, and a sea ice snapshot.

## The catalogue

```{python}
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import urllib.request, io

PARQUET = "https://data.source.coop/ausantarctic/ghrsst-mur-v2/ghrsst-mur-v2.parquet"
req = urllib.request.Request(PARQUET, headers={"User-Agent": "xvrt-docs"})
with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
    table = pq.read_table(io.BytesIO(r.read()))

rows = table.select(["datetime", "assets"]).to_pylist()
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["datetime"])
print(f"{len(rows)} items, {rows[0]['datetime']:%Y-%m-%d} .. {rows[-1]['datetime']:%Y-%m-%d}")
```

Each item is one day; each asset is one COG. Not every variable covers the
whole record:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

coverage = []
for key in rows[-1]["assets"]:
    days = [r["datetime"] for r in rows if r["assets"].get(key)]
    band = rows[-1]["assets"][key]["raster:bands"][0]
    coverage.append({"asset": key, "days": len(days),
                     "first": f"{days[0]:%Y-%m-%d}", "last": f"{days[-1]:%Y-%m-%d}",
                     "dtype": band.get("data_type"), "scale": band.get("scale"),
                     "offset": band.get("offset"), "unit": band.get("unit")})
pd.DataFrame(coverage)
```

## Build the VRT

```{python}
import time
from pathlib import Path
from xvrt import from_stac

t0 = time.time()
vrt_path = from_stac(PARQUET, Path("ghrsst-mur-v2.vrt"), block_size=[1, 512, 512])
print(f"{time.time() - t0:.1f} s, {vrt_path.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB")
```

No COG was opened: the grid, CRS, dates and each variable's storage came from
the catalogue. Days without a file for a variable are left empty and read as
nodata. The VRT is plain XML; its head:

```{python}
lines = vrt_path.read_text().splitlines()
print("\n".join(l[:110] for l in lines[:28]))
```

and a typical source:

```{python}
i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if "<Source>" in l)
print("\n".join(l[:140] for l in lines[i:i + 7]))
```

## Open it

```{python}
from osgeo import gdal

gdal.UseExceptions()
ds = gdal.OpenEx(str(vrt_path), gdal.OF_MULTIDIM_RASTER)
root = ds.GetRootGroup()
for name in root.GetMDArrayNames():
    a = root.OpenMDArray(name)
    shape = [d.GetSize() for d in a.GetDimensions()]
    print(f"{name:17s} {shape}  unit={a.GetUnit()!r}")
```

The grid and dates come back as coordinate arrays. A few helpers turn
longitude, latitude and dates into array indices, and temperatures into
degrees Celsius. The unit is whatever the catalogue records, read here rather
than assumed; only absolute temperatures are shifted from kelvin, not
differences such as the anomaly or the error estimate.

```{python}
import numpy as np

times = np.datetime64("1970-01-01") + root.OpenMDArray("time").ReadAsArray().astype("int64").astype("timedelta64[D]")

def col(lon): return int(round((lon + 179.995) / 0.01))
def row(lat): return int(round((89.995 - lat) / 0.01))
def day(date): return int(np.where(times == np.datetime64(date))[0][0])

def celsius(values, unit, absolute=True):
    kelvin = unit.lower() in ("kelvin", "k")
    return values - 273.15 if (kelvin and absolute) else values

sst = root.OpenMDArray("analysed_sst")
print(times[[0, -1]], sst.GetUnit())
```

## A regional map for one day

The Tasman Sea and Southern Ocean around Tasmania on the most recent day: one
window of one COG.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Analysed SST, 140-160E 35-50S, most recent day in the catalogue."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

west, east, north, south = 140, 160, -35, -50
t0 = time.time()
window = sst.GetUnscaled().ReadAsArray(
    array_start_idx=[len(times) - 1, row(north), col(west)],
    count=[1, row(south) - row(north), col(east) - col(west)],
)[0]
print(f"read {window.shape} in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
im = ax.imshow(celsius(window, sst.GetUnit()), extent=[west, east, south, north],
               cmap="RdYlBu_r", origin="upper")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="degrees C", shrink=0.8)
ax.set_title(f"analysed_sst {times[-1]}")
ax.set_xlabel("longitude"); ax.set_ylabel("latitude")
plt.show()
```

## One pixel through 24 years

Mid-January at 44S 150E, east of Tasmania, for every January in the record.
Each value comes from a different COG, and only those 24 files are opened:
the time is spent on one remote request per day, not on the size of the
collection.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Analysed SST on 15 January each year at 44S 150E."
def read_point(var, t, y, x):
    a = root.OpenMDArray(var)
    v = a.GetUnscaled().ReadAsArray(array_start_idx=[t, y, x], count=[1, 1, 1]).item()
    return celsius(v, a.GetUnit(), absolute=(var == "analysed_sst"))

januaries = [i for i, d in enumerate(times) if str(d).endswith("-01-15")]
t0 = time.time()
series = [read_point("analysed_sst", i, row(-44), col(150)) for i in januaries]
print(f"{len(series)} days in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

years = [int(str(times[i])[:4]) for i in januaries]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(years, series, marker="o")
ax.set_ylabel("degrees C"); ax.set_title("15 January SST at 44S 150E")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
A strided read (`array_step=[365, 1, 1]`) would be the natural way to ask for
one day per year, but in GDAL 3.13 a stride that crosses from one source to
the next fails with `arrayStartIdx[0] = ... >= 1`; stepping within a single
source works. Reading the chosen days individually, as above, avoids it.
:::

## Where a variable starts

`sst_anomaly` exists only from 2014-01-01. In the VRT it is one array over the
whole record; days before its first file are nodata:

```{python}
dates = ["2013-12-30", "2013-12-31", "2014-01-01", "2014-01-02", "2014-01-03"]
sst_vals = [read_point("analysed_sst", day(d), row(-44), col(150)) for d in dates]
anom_vals = [read_point("sst_anomaly", day(d), row(-44), col(150)) for d in dates]
pd.DataFrame({"date": dates, "analysed_sst": np.round(sst_vals, 3),
              "sst_anomaly": np.round(anom_vals, 3)})
```

## Sea ice off East Antarctica

`sea_ice_fraction` off Prydz Bay (62-70S, 70-80E) on 15 September 2025, near
the winter maximum:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Sea ice fraction, 70-80E 62-70S, 2025-09-15."
ice = root.OpenMDArray("sea_ice_fraction")
west, east, north, south = 70, 80, -62, -70
frac = ice.GetUnscaled().ReadAsArray(
    array_start_idx=[day("2025-09-15"), row(north), col(west)],
    count=[1, row(south) - row(north), col(east) - col(west)],
)[0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
im = ax.imshow(frac, extent=[west, east, south, north], cmap="Blues_r", vmin=0, vmax=1)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="fraction", shrink=0.8)
ax.set_title("sea_ice_fraction 2025-09-15  (blank: land or no ice)")
plt.show()
```

## The same cube in xarray

Any reader of GDAL's multidimensional API can use the VRT. With an xarray
backend for GDAL the five arrays become one lazy Dataset; selections are read
on demand.

```{python}
import xarray as xr

cube = xr.open_dataset(vrt_path, engine="gdalxarray")
cube
```

```{python}
v = cube.analysed_sst.sel(time="2025-02-14").sel(y=-44, x=150, method="nearest").load()
float(celsius(v.values, cube.analysed_sst.attrs.get("units", "")))
```

## Keeping it current

The VRT is a function of the catalogue, so rebuilding it whenever the
catalogue changes keeps it current: here that takes a few seconds for the
whole record, and it can be published next to the catalogue it was built
from.
